/**
 * Freedraw stroke geometry tuning constants.
 *
 * These factors are not derived analytically — they were tuned empirically by
 * visually comparing rendered strokes until they matched the desired feel.
 * Treat them as magic numbers backed by visual verification.
 */
const VARIABLE_WIDTH_FREEDRAW = {
  /** Stroke size relative to `strokeWidth` for pressure-sensitive strokes. */
  SIZE_FACTOR: 4.25,
  THINNING: 0.6,
  SMOOTHING: 0.5,
} as const;

const CONSTANT_WIDTH_FREEDRAW = {
  /** Stroke size relative to `strokeWidth` for uniform (laser) strokes. */
  SIZE_FACTOR: 1.4,
} as const;

const getFreedrawStreamline = (element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement) =>
  element.strokeOptions?.streamline ?? DEFAULT_STROKE_STREAMLINE;

/**
 * Pressure-sensitive (variable width) freedraw outline, rendered with
 * perfect-freehand. This is the original Excalidraw freedraw look.
 */
const getVariableWidthFreedrawOutline = (
  element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement,
): [number, number][] => {
  // If input points are empty (should they ever be?) return a dot
  const inputPoints = element.simulatePressure
    ? element.points
    : element.points.length
    ? element.points.map(
        ([x, y], i) => [x, y, element.pressures[i]] as [number, number, number],
      )
    : [[0, 0, 0.5]];

  return getStroke(inputPoints as number[][], {
    simulatePressure: element.simulatePressure,
    size: element.strokeWidth * VARIABLE_WIDTH_FREEDRAW.SIZE_FACTOR,
    thinning: VARIABLE_WIDTH_FREEDRAW.THINNING,
    smoothing: VARIABLE_WIDTH_FREEDRAW.SMOOTHING,
    streamline: getFreedrawStreamline(element),
    easing: (t) => Math.sin((t * Math.PI) / 2), // https://easings.net/#easeOutSine
    last: true,
  }) as [number, number][];
};

const createLaserPointer = (element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement) =>
  new LaserPointer({
    size: element.strokeWidth * CONSTANT_WIDTH_FREEDRAW.SIZE_FACTOR,
    streamline: getFreedrawStreamline(element),
    simplify: 0,
    sizeMapping: (details) => Math.max(0.1, details.pressure),
  });

/**
 * Uniform (constant width) freedraw outline, rendered with the laser-pointer
 * geometry. Pressure is pinned to 1 so the stroke keeps a constant width.
 */
const getConstantWidthFreedrawOutline = (
  element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement,
): [number, number][] => {
  const laserPointer = createLaserPointer(element);
  element.points.map(([x, y]) => laserPointer.addPoint([x, y, 1]));

  return laserPointer
    .getStrokeOutline()
    .map(([x, y]) => [x, y] as [number, number]);
};

): [number, number][] => {
  // Unknown/absent variability falls back to the original variable rendering.
  return element.strokeOptions?.variability === "constant"
    ? getConstantWidthFreedrawOutline(element)
    : getVariableWidthFreedrawOutline(element);

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:08:44Z)**_

The freehand tool stores the raw pointer points exactly as you drew them. All of the smoothing happens later, each time the stroke is drawn on screen.

## 1. Capturing the stroke (`packages/excalidraw/components/App.tsx`)

- **Pointer down (~line 9676):** `newFreeDrawElement()` creates a `freedraw` element whose first point is `(0,0)`, relative to the element's `x/y`. Two things are decided here:
  - `simulatePressure = event.pressure === 0.5`. A mouse always reports a pressure of 0.5, so a mouse means "fake the pressure." A pen reports real values.
  - `strokeOptions.streamline` is `DEFAULT_STROKE_STREAMLINE` (0.5) for a mouse and `DEFAULT_STROKE_STREAMLINE_PRECISE` (0.2) for a pen or touch. Pen input is already accurate, so it gets less smoothing. Both values are in `packages/common/src/constants.ts:578`.
- **Pointer move (~line 11340):** each move adds the cursor position (relative to the element) to `points`. If the stroke uses real pressure, `event.pressure` is added to `pressures`. A point identical to the previous one is dropped. Nothing else happens to the points here.
- **Pointer up (~line 11835):** one last point is added. If the stroke is a single click, the point is nudged by 0.0001 so the dot isn't treated as having zero size. Then `actionFinalize` runs.

## 2. Turning points into a smooth shape (`packages/element/src/shape.ts:1225–1336`)

`getFreedrawOutlinePoints()` builds the outline of the stroke: a closed polygon that is filled in, rather than a line drawn with a fixed width. It has two modes, chosen by `strokeOptions.variability`.

### Variable width (the default) uses the [`perfect-freehand`](https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-freehand) library

```ts
getStroke(inputPoints, {
  simulatePressure: element.simulatePressure,
  size: element.strokeWidth * 4.25,
  thinning: 0.6,
  smoothing: 0.5,
  streamline: element.strokeOptions?.streamline ?? 0.5,
  easing: (t) => Math.sin((t * Math.PI) / 2), // easeOutSine
  last: true,
});
```

Each setting contributes to the smoothing:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`streamline`** | This is the main smoothing step. Each input point is pulled part of the way from the previous smoothed point toward the new raw point, roughly `p' = lerp(prev, p, 1 − streamline)`. This is a running average, so hand jitter gets filtered out. A higher value gives a smoother line that trails further behind the cursor. That's why a mouse gets 0.5 and a pen gets 0.2. |
| **`smoothing`** | Softens the outline's edges: points closer together than `size × smoothing` count less when the left and right edges are calculated. |
| **`thinning` + `simulatePressure`** | Controls how much pressure changes the width. With a real pen, the recorded `pressures` are used. With simulated pressure, the library estimates it from speed, so fast movement draws a thinner line. |
| **`easing`** | The easeOutSine curve maps pressure to width, so the width changes gradually instead of in a straight proportion. |
| **`last: true`** | Treats the stroke as finished, so the end gets a properly rounded cap. |

The size, thinning and smoothing numbers are documented in the code as values tuned by eye (`VARIABLE_WIDTH_FREEDRAW`).

### Constant width uses `packages/laser-pointer`

`getConstantWidthFreedrawOutline()` passes every point into a `LaserPointer` with the same `streamline` value and `simplify: 0`. It pins pressure to 1 so the width never changes. The size is `strokeWidth × 1.4`.

## 3. Converting the outline to a curved path (`shape.ts:1315`)

`getSvgPathFromStroke()` turns the polygon into an SVG path made of quadratic Bézier curves (`Q`). Each outline point is a control point, and each curve ends at the midpoint between that point and the next one. Because every curve starts and ends at a midpoint, the joins have no sharp corners. This is a second, geometric layer of smoothing on top of the streamline step. Coordinates are also cut to 2 decimal places.

That path string is filled on the canvas with `context.fill(new Path2D(shape))` in `renderElement.ts:521` and is also used for SVG export. If the stroke forms a closed loop and has a background fill, `simplify(points, 0.75)` (Ramer–Douglas–Peucker) thins the points first. Rough.js then draws the fill as a curve (`shape.ts:997`).

## In short

**Raw points are stored → streamline running average filters jitter → perfect-freehand builds a pressure-shaped outline → the outline is drawn as a chain of quadratic Béziers through midpoints → the result is filled.** The original raw points are never changed, so you could change the smoothing settings later and existing drawings would be redrawn with them.

import React from "react";

import { pointFrom } from "@excalidraw/math";
import {
  getSizeFromPoints,
  PATH_PLAYBACK_HOLD_MS,
  reseed,
} from "@excalidraw/common";

import type { ExcalidrawPathElement } from "@excalidraw/element/types";

import { Excalidraw } from "../index";

import { act, render } from "./test-utils";
import { Pointer } from "./helpers/ui";
import { API } from "./helpers/api";

const { h } = window;
const mouse = new Pointer("mouse");

const getElement = (id: string) => h.elements.find((el) => el.id === id)!;

const setupPathWithTarget = () => {
  const rectangle = API.createElement({
    type: "rectangle",
    x: 0,
    y: 0,
    width: 100,
    height: 100,
    backgroundColor: "#000000",
  });
  const points = [pointFrom(0, 0), pointFrom(100, 0)];
  const path = API.createElement({
    type: "path",
    x: 300,
    y: 300,
    ...getSizeFromPoints(points),
    points: points as ExcalidrawPathElement["points"],
    targetElementId: rectangle.id,
  });
  API.setElements([rectangle, path]);
  return { rectangle, path };
};

beforeEach(async () => {
  localStorage.clear();
  reseed(7);
  mouse.reset();
  await render(<Excalidraw handleKeyboardGlobally={true} />);
});

afterEach(() => {
  vi.useRealTimers();
  vi.restoreAllMocks();
});

describe("press-and-hold path playback", () => {
  it("doesn't leave the target and path stuck to the pointer after release", () => {
    const { rectangle, path } = setupPathWithTarget();

    // isolate the pointer handling from the animation itself
    const preview = vi
      .spyOn(h.app.pathPlayback, "preview")
      .mockImplementation(() => {});
    vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["setTimeout", "clearTimeout"] });

    mouse.downAt(50, 50);
    act(() => {
      vi.advanceTimersByTime(PATH_PLAYBACK_HOLD_MS);
    });
    expect(preview).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1);

    // moving while still holding must not drag
    mouse.moveTo(10, 10);
    mouse.upAt(10, 10);

    // moving with no button held after release must not drag either
    mouse.moveTo(150, 150);
    mouse.moveTo(200, 200);

    expect(getElement(rectangle.id).x).toBe(0);
    expect(getElement(rectangle.id).y).toBe(0);
    expect(getElement(path.id).x).toBe(300);
    expect(getElement(path.id).y).toBe(300);
  });

  it("still drags the target on a normal press after a hold", () => {
    const { rectangle } = setupPathWithTarget();

    vi.spyOn(h.app.pathPlayback, "preview").mockImplementation(() => {});
    vi.useFakeTimers({ toFake: ["setTimeout", "clearTimeout"] });

    mouse.downAt(50, 50);
    act(() => {
      vi.advanceTimersByTime(PATH_PLAYBACK_HOLD_MS);
    });
    mouse.upAt(50, 50);

    // a fresh press-and-drag should behave like a regular move
    mouse.downAt(50, 50);
    mouse.moveTo(80, 90);
    mouse.upAt(80, 90);

    expect(getElement(rectangle.id).x).toBe(30);
    expect(getElement(rectangle.id).y).toBe(40);
  });
});

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:15:44Z)**_

Pointer jumps cause these artifacts because nothing in the pipeline fills in the gap a jump leaves. Excalidraw records one point per move event, and perfect-freehand's smoothing works on those samples one at a time. When the pointer jumps, the stroke gets a single long segment, often with a sudden change of direction. Each later stage then turns that long segment into a hard edge. I found this by reading the code; I haven't reproduced it in a test yet.

### 1. Nothing fills the gap at capture time (`App.tsx` ~11340)

The move handler drops a point only if it exactly repeats the previous one. It never adds points across a large gap, and it doesn't use `getCoalescedEvents()` (that call appears nowhere in `packages/`). A jump comes from things like a dropped frame, a slow render, a pen leaving and re-entering hover range, or touch-to-pen handoff. Whatever the cause, it becomes one long segment between two samples.

### 2. Streamline smooths samples, not distance

In perfect-freehand 1.2.0 (`getStrokePoints`), each new point is a fixed fraction of the way from the previous smoothed point to the new raw point:

```js
t = 0.15 + (1 - streamline) * 0.85; // 0.575 for mouse, 0.83 for pen
p = lerp(prevSmoothed, raw, t);
```

That fraction doesn't depend on how far apart the points are, so a 100px jump moves just as abruptly as a 2px step, and the smoothed path still contains a long straight run. Also, because of `last: true`, the final point is the raw point with no smoothing, so a jump right before pointer-up stays fully sharp.

### 3. Simulated pressure (mouse) changes the width abruptly

When pressure is simulated, perfect-freehand estimates it from the distance between samples, not from time:

```js
s = min(1, distance / size); // size = strokeWidth * 4.25
pressure = prev + (1 - s - prev) * (s * 0.275);
```

With `strokeWidth` 2, `size` is 8.5, so any segment longer than about 8.5px counts as top speed. Pressure then drops by 27.5% in that single step. The stroke's half-width (`m`) shrinks just as suddenly, and because `thinning` is set to 0.6 the change is large. The outline shows it as a visible step in width.

### 4. Sudden direction changes trigger semicircle caps (`getStrokeOutlinePoints`)

```js
if (dot(vector, prevVector) < 0 || dot(vector, nextVector) < 0) {
  // insert a 13-step semicircle around this point on both sides
}
```

A jump, or a single bad sample that goes out and comes back, often turns the stroke by more than 90°. Each such point gets a cap of radius `m`. A spike therefore becomes two rounded blobs joined by thin straight edges, which looks like a lump stuck on the stroke.

When the turn is sharp but under 90°, no cap is added. The left and right edge points are offset along a blend of the incoming and outgoing directions. Next to a long segment, the inner edge can then overshoot and cross the opposite side. The outline polygon folds over itself, and filling it shows triangular notches.

### 5. The outline has no extra points along long segments

Each edge gets a new outline point only after moving at least `size * smoothing` (`te`) from the last one, and only at actual sample positions. A long segment therefore has exactly two outline points, one at each end.

### 6. The curve fitting only smooths between points that exist (`shape.ts` `getSvgPathFromStroke`)

The path is a chain of quadratic Béziers that pass through midpoints between outline points, with each outline point as a control point. That rounds corners only when the points are close together. With two points far apart, the curve is just a straight line ending in a sharp turn. Combined with the width step (3), the caps (4) and the folds (4), that gives the "blocky polygon" look.

Constant-width strokes (`packages/laser-pointer`) have the same weakness. Their streamline is also a fixed-fraction blend per sample (`state.ts:77`), and corners get `Math.PI / 16` arcs. They avoid the pressure problem, though, because pressure is pinned to 1.

### Ways to fix it, roughly from most to least effective

1. **Fill large gaps before smoothing.** In the move handler, or before `getStroke` in `getVariableWidthFreedrawOutline`, add points every ~`size/2` across any segment longer than `size`. Every stage downstream then works with closely spaced points.
2. **Use `event.getCoalescedEvents()`** in the freedraw move handler to recover the samples the browser merged.
3. **Throw out single-sample spikes.** Drop a point that jumps out and immediately reverses direction.
4. **Limit how fast simulated pressure can change**, so one long segment can't thin the stroke much at once.

Option 1 fixes most of it alone, and it changes only how strokes are drawn, not the saved data, so existing drawings would improve too. I can implement it with a regression test that draws a stroke with a jump and checks the outline for spikes or folds.

import { pointFrom } from "@excalidraw/math";
import { newFreeDrawElement } from "../../src/newElement";
import { getFreedrawOutlinePoints } from "../../src/shape";

const mk = (pts: [number, number][], variability: "variable" | "constant", simulatePressure = true) =>
  newFreeDrawElement({
    type: "freedraw", x: 0, y: 0, strokeWidth: 2,
    simulatePressure, points: pts.map(([x, y]) => pointFrom(x, y)) as any,
    pressures: simulatePressure ? [] : pts.map(() => 0.5),
    strokeOptions: { variability, streamline: 0.5 },
  } as any);

const segX = (x0: number, x1: number, step: number, y = 0) => {
  const o: [number, number][] = [];
  for (let x = x0; x <= x1; x += step) o.push([x, y + Math.sin(x / 15) * 5]);
  return o;
};

const segInt = (a: number[], b: number[], c: number[], d: number[]) => {
  const o = (p: number[], q: number[], r: number[]) => Math.sign((q[0]-p[0])*(r[1]-p[1])-(q[1]-p[1])*(r[0]-p[0]));
  return o(a,b,c)*o(a,b,d) < 0 && o(c,d,a)*o(c,d,b) < 0;
};
const metrics = (out: number[][], center: [number, number][]) => {
  let maxEdge = 0, ints = 0, maxDist = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < out.length; i++) {
    const a = out[i], b = out[(i+1)%out.length];
    maxEdge = Math.max(maxEdge, Math.hypot(a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1]));
    for (let j = i+2; j < out.length; j++) {
      if (i === 0 && j === out.length-1) continue;
      if (segInt(a, b, out[j], out[(j+1)%out.length])) ints++;
    }
  }
  // turning: max abs angle change
  let maxTurn = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < out.length; i++) {
    const a = out[(i-1+out.length)%out.length], b = out[i], c = out[(i+1)%out.length];
    const t = Math.abs(Math.atan2(Math.sin(Math.atan2(c[1]-b[1],c[0]-b[0]) - Math.atan2(b[1]-a[1],b[0]-a[0])), Math.cos(Math.atan2(c[1]-b[1],c[0]-b[0]) - Math.atan2(b[1]-a[1],b[0]-a[0]))));
    maxTurn = Math.max(maxTurn, t);
  }
  return { n: out.length, maxEdge: +maxEdge.toFixed(1), ints, maxTurnDeg: +(maxTurn*180/Math.PI).toFixed(0) };
};

it("probe", () => {
  const smooth = segX(0, 300, 3);

```typescript
import { pointFrom } from "@excalidraw/math";

import type { LocalPoint } from "@excalidraw/math";

import { newFreeDrawElement } from "../src/newElement";
import { getFreedrawOutlinePoints } from "../src/shape";

import type { ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement } from "../src/types";

type Point = [number, number];

const STROKE_WIDTH = 2;

// longest straight edge the outline polygon may contain. Densely sampled
// strokes stay well under this (~8px variable, ~4px constant at
// strokeWidth 2); anything longer renders as a visible flat facet
const MAX_OUTLINE_EDGE = 12;

// the stroke right after a pointer jump must keep at least this fraction of
// its regular half-width (simulated pressure must not collapse it)
const MIN_WIDTH_RATIO_AFTER_JUMP = 0.75;

const createFreedraw = (
  points: Point[],
  variability: "variable" | "constant",
) =>
  newFreeDrawElement({
    type: "freedraw",
    x: 0,
    y: 0,
    strokeWidth: STROKE_WIDTH,
    simulatePressure: true,
    points: points.map(([x, y]) => pointFrom<LocalPoint>(x, y)),
    strokeOptions: { variability, streamline: 0.5 },
  });

// gently wavy horizontal run, sampled every `step` px like pointermove events
const wavyRun = (fromX: number, toX: number, step = 3): Point[] => {
  const points: Point[] = [];
  for (let x = fromX; x <= toX; x += step) {
    points.push([x, Math.sin(x / 15) * 5]);
  }
  return points;
};

const SMOOTH_STROKE = wavyRun(0, 300);

// pointer jumps 120px between two consecutive samples (dropped frames, pen
// leaving hover range, ...) and then carries on in the same direction
const STRAIGHT_JUMP_STROKE = [...wavyRun(0, 120), ...wavyRun(240, 300)];

// pointer jumps and the stroke continues in a different direction
const TURNING_JUMP_STROKE: Point[] = [...wavyRun(0, 120)];
for (let i = 0; i <= 40; i++) {
  TURNING_JUMP_STROKE.push([200 + i * 2, 80 + i * 3]);
}

const getMaxOutlineEdge = (element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement) => {
  const outline = getFreedrawOutlinePoints(element);
  let maxEdge = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < outline.length; i++) {
    const [ax, ay] = outline[i];
    const [bx, by] = outline[(i + 1) % outline.length];
    maxEdge = Math.max(maxEdge, Math.hypot(bx - ax, by - ay));
  }
  return maxEdge;
};

const distanceToSegment = (
  [px, py]: Point,
  [ax, ay]: Point,
  [bx, by]: Point,
) => {
  const dx = bx - ax;
  const dy = by - ay;
  const lengthSq = dx * dx + dy * dy;
  const t = lengthSq
    ? Math.max(0, Math.min(1, ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / lengthSq))
    : 0;
  return Math.hypot(px - ax - t * dx, py - ay - t * dy);
};

const isInsidePolygon = ([px, py]: Point, polygon: Point[]) => {
  let inside = false;
  for (let i = 0, j = polygon.length - 1; i < polygon.length; j = i++) {
    const [ax, ay] = polygon[i];
    const [bx, by] = polygon[j];
    if (ay > py !== by > py && px < ((bx - ax) * (py - ay)) / (by - ay) + ax) {
      inside = !inside;
    }
  }
  return inside;
};

/**
 * Half-width of the rendered stroke at each drawn point within [fromX, toX]:
 * distance from the point to the nearest outline edge, or 0 if the outline
 * doesn't even cover the point.
 */
const getHalfWidths = (
  element: ExcalidrawFreeDrawElement,
  fromX: number,
  toX: number,
) => {
  const outline = getFreedrawOutlinePoints(element);
  return element.points
    .filter(([x]) => x >= fromX && x <= toX)
    .map(([x, y]): number => {
      const point: Point = [x, y];
      if (!isInsidePolygon(point, outline)) {
        return 0;
      }
      let min = Infinity;
      for (let i = 0; i < outline.length; i++) {
        min = Math.min(
          min,
          distanceToSegment(
            point,
            outline[i],
            outline[(i + 1) % outline.length],
          ),
        );
      }
      return min;
    });
};

const median = (values: number[]) => {
  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  return sorted[Math.floor(sorted.length / 2)];
};

describe("freedraw outline with pointer position jumps", () => {
  describe.each(["variable", "constant"] as const)(
    "%s width stroke",
    (variability) => {
      it("has no long straight outline edges for a densely sampled stroke", () => {
        expect(
          getMaxOutlineEdge(createFreedraw(SMOOTH_STROKE, variability)),
        ).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_OUTLINE_EDGE);
      });

      it.each([
        ["straight", STRAIGHT_JUMP_STROKE],
        ["turning", TURNING_JUMP_STROKE],
      ])(
        "has no long straight outline edges across a %s pointer jump",
        (_, points) => {
          expect(
            getMaxOutlineEdge(createFreedraw(points, variability)),
          ).toBeLessThanOrEqual(MAX_OUTLINE_EDGE);
        },
      );
    },
  );

  describe("variable width stroke with simulated pressure", () => {
    const expectWidthHeldAfterX240 = (points: Point[]) => {
      const element = createFreedraw(points, "variable");
      const regularHalfWidth = median(getHalfWidths(element, 30, 110));
      const halfWidthsAfterJump = getHalfWidths(element, 240, 270);

      expect(halfWidthsAfterJump.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);
      expect(Math.min(...halfWidthsAfterJump)).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(
        regularHalfWidth * MIN_WIDTH_RATIO_AFTER_JUMP,
      );
    };

    it("keeps a constant width along a densely sampled stroke", () => {
      expectWidthHeldAfterX240(SMOOTH_STROKE);
    });

    it("doesn't pinch the stroke right after a pointer jump", () => {
      expectWidthHeldAfterX240(STRAIGHT_JUMP_STROKE);
    });
  });
});
```

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:33:18Z)**_

I added the regression test in `packages/element/tests/freedrawOutline.test.ts`. As intended, it fails on the current code: 5 of the 8 tests fail and 3 pass. Prettier, ESLint and the TypeScript check are all clean. Nothing is committed.

I first ran some throwaway experiments (since deleted) to find what actually tells a broken stroke from a good one. Two ideas didn't work. Counting where the outline crosses itself is no good, because normal strokes already do that at their end caps. Measuring how far the outline strays from the drawn line is no good either: across a jump, both the outline and the raw input follow the same straight line.

The tests build freedraw elements with simulated pressure and call `getFreedrawOutlinePoints` directly. They use three strokes: a smooth wavy stroke sampled every 3px, the same stroke with a 120px gap that then carries on straight, and one with a gap that then turns. They check two things:

| Check | Smooth stroke | After a jump (current code) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Longest straight edge in the outline** must be ≤ 12px, for both variable and constant width | 7.9px / 3.6px ✓ | 74px, 70px / 62px, 57px ✗ |
| **Stroke width at x = 240–270** (just after the jump) must stay ≥ 75% of the normal width (variable width only) | ~6.5, steady ✓ | drops to 2.8 against a normal ~6.4 ✗ |

- **Long straight edges** are the blocky, flat sides you see. With a jump there's nothing to smooth across the gap, so the outline becomes long straight lines.
- **The width check** catches the pinch: the long gap fools the pressure estimate into thinning the stroke, and it takes about 30px to recover.

The smooth strokes pass both checks, which confirms the limits aren't too strict for normal drawing. The limits (`MAX_OUTLINE_EDGE`, `MIN_WIDTH_RATIO_AFTER_JUMP`) are named constants at the top of the file with comments.

The fix I suggested earlier (adding extra points across large gaps before smoothing) should make all 8 tests pass. Want me to implement it?

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 21:52:47Z)**_

I've fixed the jump artifacts. All 8 new tests in `packages/element/tests/freedrawOutline.test.ts` now pass, the typecheck is clean, and `yarn test:update` passes everything except one unrelated test (below). Nothing is committed.

**What I changed:** I added a helper, `getFreedrawInputPoints()`, in `packages/element/src/shape.ts`. Before a stroke is smoothed, it looks for any gap between consecutive points larger than **16 × `strokeWidth`** (32px at the default bold width). It fills each one with evenly spaced points about **2 × `strokeWidth`** apart. With real pen pressure, the pressure is blended evenly across the gap too. Both stroke modes use it: the variable-width mode (perfect-freehand) and the constant-width mode (laser pointer).

- **Only jumps are filled, not every gap.** Simulated pressure deliberately thins fast strokes, and it works out speed from the distance between points. Filling every gap would remove that effect from normal fast drawing. Very large gaps are the ones that come from dropped frames or the pen re-entering hover range, not real hand movement. So strokes without jumps, including every existing drawing, render exactly as before. The full suite passing with no snapshot changes is consistent with that.
- **Saved drawings are unchanged.** The extra points are only used for drawing the stroke. Saved points, bounds and hit-testing are untouched.
- **The 16× and 2× values are my judgement, not measured.** They're named constants (`FREEDRAW_POINTER_JUMP`) next to the existing tuning values. One limitation: a jump just under the threshold still gets a straight run of up to about 16 × `strokeWidth`. That's smaller relative to the stroke's width, but not gone.

**The failing test:** `packages/excalidraw/tests/pathPlaybackHold.test.tsx` (the untracked press-and-hold motion-path test) fails with `expected 150 to be +0`. It fails the same way with my change stashed, so it isn't caused by this fix. It looks like the unfinished work this branch is named for.

I haven't checked this by drawing in the app. A pointer jump is hard to produce by hand; the closest test would be drawing fast while the browser is busy and checking for flat facets or a thin pinch right after a gap.

I couldn't find anything in the code that would do this. The freedraw tool doesn't even have a way to.

1. **The app can't move your mouse cursor.** Browsers don't let a web page move the system cursor. Only your hardware, Windows, or a driver can do that.
2. **New points only come from real pointer events.** The freedraw move handler (`App.tsx` ~11341) adds a point only when the browser sends a `pointermove`. If the pointer isn't moving, no events arrive and the stroke can't grow. My jump fix doesn't change this either: it only adds drawing-only points between two points you actually drew, and never past the last one.
3. **Nothing scrolls the canvas while you draw.** I checked everything that changes the scroll position. Each one is triggered by a wheel, keyboard, pinch, scrollbar or pan input. The only automatic motion is the snap-back animation for viewport locking (`scrollConstraints`), and the web app doesn't turn that on. There are no timers, auto-scroll or "keep moving" features in the drawing code.

So the most likely cause is outside Excalidraw:

- **If the cursor itself keeps moving** (you can see it slide), the input is coming from your device or Windows. Common causes are pen hover drift on a tablet, a touchscreen picking up your palm, a sticky trackpad, or a controller or joystick plugged in. A quick test: hold still in Paint or on the desktop. If the cursor drifts there too, it's the hardware.
- **If only the line keeps extending downward**, something is still sending pointer events. On a pen or touch screen, your palm or wrist can register as a second contact below where you're drawing.
- **If it's the page or canvas that moves**, I'd want to know whether you're running excalidraw.com, your local dev server, or the library inside another page. The surrounding page could be scrolling.

To narrow it down, which of these is it: the cursor arrow moving, the line growing, or the whole canvas scrolling? And are you using a mouse, a trackpad, a pen or touch? With that, I can add logging to the freedraw move handler to print each pointer event and confirm where the movement comes from.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 23:23:21Z)**_

If the arrow itself keeps moving, the movement is coming from your hardware or from Windows, not from Excalidraw. A web page can't move the system cursor. Excalidraw only reacts to the movement once it happens, which is why the line follows the cursor to the bottom of the screen.

**If you're drawing on a laptop touchpad, the likely cause is "edge motion".** Many touchpad drivers (Synaptics, ELAN, some Dell and HP models) have it. While you're dragging, if your finger reaches the edge of the pad, the driver keeps moving the cursor in that direction until you lift. A downward curve pushes your finger toward the bottom edge, so the cursor keeps sliding to the bottom of the screen even after you stop. It only happens while the button is held, so you'd see it while drawing and not when just moving the cursor around.

To fix it:

1. Open Settings → Bluetooth & devices → Touchpad, or the touchpad's own app (Synaptics, ELAN, Dell or HP Touchpad settings).
2. Look for **Edge motion** or **Edge scrolling / extended edge**, and **Drag lock** or **tap-and-drag**, and turn them off.
3. If you only find "More touchpad settings", it's under Mouse Properties → the touchpad or device tab → Settings.

If it isn't the touchpad:

- **Pen or tablet:** a worn nib, or the pen resting near the screen, can drift while hovering. Try lifting the pen fully away, and check the tablet driver for hover or pressure settings.
- **Something else plugged in:** a game controller, a second mouse, or remote-control software can move the cursor. Unplug or close them and try again.
- **Quick check:** hold the button down and draw a downward curve in Paint. If the cursor runs away there too, it's definitely the device or its settings.

What are you drawing with? If it's a touchpad, tell me the laptop model and I can point you to where the setting lives.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 23:35:08Z)**_

Both are in place now, and all 8 regression tests pass. The test file was still there, but my earlier fix to `packages/element/src/shape.ts` had been removed from your working tree. It wasn't in a stash, so I re-applied it.

- **Regression test** (`packages/element/tests/freedrawOutline.test.ts`): it builds strokes with a 120px jump, one that carries on straight and one that turns, alongside a smooth stroke as a control. It checks that the stroke's outline has no straight edge longer than 12px, and that the stroke doesn't thin out right after the jump. Without the fix, the 5 jump tests fail; with it, all 8 pass.
- **Fix** (`shape.ts`): before smoothing, any gap between two points wider than 16 × the stroke width is filled with evenly spaced points about 2 × the stroke width apart. Real pen pressure is blended across the gap too. Both freedraw styles, variable and constant width, go through this. Only the drawing uses the extra points; the saved points stay as drawn. Normal fast strokes are below the threshold, so their intended thinning and the look of existing drawings don't change.

Prettier, ESLint and `yarn test:typecheck` are clean. `yarn test:update` passes 1966 tests with no snapshot changes. The one failure is `pathPlaybackHold.test.tsx`, which already failed before this change and comes from the unfinished press-and-hold motion-path work. Nothing is committed.

I only implemented the first of the four fixes I suggested, because it handles most of the problem alone. The other three are still open: reading the samples the browser merged with `getCoalescedEvents()`, dropping single-point spikes, and limiting how fast simulated pressure can change. I can add any of them if you want.

This fixes the blocky outlines around jumps. It doesn't affect the cursor sliding to the bottom of the screen, which comes from your device or Windows settings, not Excalidraw.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 23:56:28Z)**_

I found and fixed the cause of the small lines. It's a rounding bug in how the stroke is turned into an SVG path, not in the smoothing.

**What was happening:** before drawing, `getSvgPathFromStroke` in `packages/element/src/shape.ts` cut every coordinate to 2 decimals using a regex on the text of the number. When you press and nudge straight down (or straight sideways), some outline points should land exactly on 0. Floating-point error makes them tiny values like `3.43e-16`, and JavaScript writes those in scientific notation. The regex kept `3.43` and threw away the `e-16`. So a point that belonged at 0 was drawn 3–4.5px away, past the edge of the dot. Those stray points are the little lines.

- It shows up with the **constant-width** stroke style, which is the app's default. The variable-width style never produced these tiny values in my tests.
- It's most visible on a press-and-nudge, because the bad points are near the start of the stroke and the dot is small. At the default bold width the stroke's half-width is only 2.8px, so a 3.4px error sticks out.

**Fix:** each coordinate is now rounded as a number (`Number(x.toFixed(2))`) before the path text is built, so noise like `3.4e-16` becomes `0`. The only other change is that coordinates now round to the nearest 0.01 instead of being cut off; no snapshots changed.

**Regression test:** I added 6 tests to `packages/element/tests/freedrawOutline.test.ts`. They nudge the pointer down by 1px, down by 3px and right, in both stroke styles, and check that every coordinate in the path stays inside the stroke's outline. Before the fix, the 3 constant-width cases failed with `expected 3.42 to be less than or equal to 3.31`. All 14 tests in the file now pass, and Prettier, ESLint and the typecheck are clean.

**Full suite:** 1971 tests pass and 2 fail.

- `pathPlaybackHold.test.tsx` is the same failure from before my changes.
- `excalidraw-app/tests/visibleExports.test.tsx` failed once in the full run. It passed when run alone twice with my change and once without it, so it looks flaky under load rather than caused by this.

I haven't checked this by drawing in the app. Nothing is committed; the jump fix from earlier is still in place alongside this one.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-23 00:17:39Z)**_

I made two fixes to how freehand strokes are drawn, both in `packages/element/src/shape.ts`, and added one test file. Nothing is committed.

## 1. Blocky edges after a pointer jump

**Problem:** sometimes the pointer jumps a long way between two samples (for example after dropped frames or a pen re-entering range). Both stroke styles smooth one sample at a time, so the jump became one long straight segment. That showed up as flat, blocky edges, and with simulated pressure the stroke also thinned out sharply just after the jump.

**Fix:** a new helper, `getFreedrawInputPoints()`, fills any gap longer than 16 × the stroke width with evenly spaced points about 2 × the stroke width apart. With a real pen, pressure is blended across the gap too. Both stroke styles use it.

- Shorter gaps are left alone, so fast normal strokes keep their intended thinning and existing drawings look the same.
- Only the drawing uses the extra points. Saved points, bounds and hit-testing are unchanged.
- The two values are named constants (`FREEDRAW_POINTER_JUMP`) and were chosen by judgement.

## 2. Small lines sticking out of a pressed dot

**Problem:** `getSvgPathFromStroke` cut coordinates to 2 decimals with a regex on the number's text. Floating-point noise like `3.43e-16` became `3.42`, because the regex dropped the `e-16`. That pushed outline points 3–4.5px out of place. It mostly affected the default constant-width style when you press and nudge straight down or sideways.

**Fix:** each coordinate is now rounded as a number (`Number(x.toFixed(2))`) before the path text is built, so the noise becomes `0`. Coordinates now round instead of being cut off, a difference of at most 0.01; no snapshots changed.

## 3. Regression tests: `packages/element/tests/freedrawOutline.test.ts` (new, 14 tests)

- **Pointer jumps (8 tests):** a smooth stroke and strokes with a 120px jump, straight and turning, in both stroke styles. They check that no outline edge is longer than 12px and that the stroke keeps at least 75% of its width after the jump. Before the fix, 5 failed.
- **Pressed dot (6 tests):** nudges of 1px down, 3px down and 3px right, in both styles. They check that every path coordinate stays inside the stroke's outline. Before the fix, the 3 constant-width cases failed.

## Verification

All 14 new tests pass, and Prettier, ESLint and the typecheck are clean. In the full `yarn test:update` run, 1971 tests pass and 2 fail:

- `pathPlaybackHold.test.tsx`: an untracked test from the unfinished motion-path work that also fails without my changes.
- `visibleExports.test.tsx`: failed once in the full run but passed every time it ran alone, so it looks flaky.

Neither fix has been checked by drawing in the app.

The cursor sliding to the bottom of the screen needed no code change: it comes from your hardware or Windows, most likely touchpad edge motion.
